newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanian hopes Israel can turn bananas into fish.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian hopes Israel can turn bananas into fish.

text.p: A Jordanian landowner whose Dead Sea banana plantations have been losing money for decades could be rescued by Israeli technology and U.S. cash.

Sheikh Sami al-Adwan owns hundreds of hectares of farmland in the Jordan Valley and hopes Israeli know-how can help him convert the loss-making land into a base for money-spinning projects like fish farming, industry and tourism.

"We want to get our land working, and they (Israelis) have the technology," Adwan told Reuters on Sunday as he hosted an Israeli and U.S. business delegation to his farm, which once made up part of the frontline of Arab-Israeli conflict.
"If they want to exploit it all, we'll give it to them."
He said traditional crops like vegetables, citrus fruit and bananas gave poor returns and farmers were heavily in debt.

Adwan, wearing a flowing Arab head-dress and a golden dagger, discussed business opportunities with Israeli businessman Zvi Shorer, chairman of the chamber of businesses in the northern Israeli town of Beit Shean.
Shorer said up to 50 businesses in Beit Shean were looking for opportunities in Jordan because of its cheap labour and because it could act as a bridge into other Arab markets.
The first clear business opportunities in the Jordan Valley were tourism and fish farming, already a success in Israel, he said.
"The sheikh has salty water that has no (agricultural) use...but we can make a fortune out of this water, breeding fish," he said.

Businessmen say Israeli companies have set up at least a dozen partnership projects in Jordan, most of them in textiles, since the two countries signed a peace treaty in 1994 which ended a 46-year state of war.
But popular hostility to Israel, especially since the election of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last year, means cooperation with the Jewish state usually remains low profile.
An Israeli trade show last month in Amman prompted demonstrations outside the exhibition hall. Jordan's powerful Engineers Union has a blacklist to deter firms from dealing with Israel.

Multimillion dollar deals agreed in the wave of optimism after the peace deal was signed have fallen by the wayside, including a $300 million project for Jordan to process gas from the Gulf state of Qatar for sale to Israel.
Adwan, whose land extends to within five km (three miles) of the Israeli-controlled West Bank border, said the Jewish state was no longer an enemy.

"For 30 years this land was a theatre of war and the first line of defence for Jordan and the whole Arab world," he said. "This land and its people suffered the tragedies of war... The time has come to reap the benefits of peace".
Shorer was accompanied by leaders of the Cleveland-based U.S.-Ohio Chamber of Commerce who said they could help raise capital to get Israeli-Jordanian projects off the ground.

He said opportunities for Israel to subcontract work in Jordan included a textile factory which could employ up to 200 people and plants to make car spare parts employing 50 people, as well as factories to produce anything from irrigation pipes to software.
Adwan said he was also considering a mineral-water factory.
No deals have been finalised, but Shorer said the first agreement he expected to sign would be a contract to turn a nearby farm into a tourist motel.
"We'll call it the Honey Inn," he said.
